editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: Wherever Ptolemy son of Lagus and Aristobulus son of Aristobulus have written the same things about Alexander son of Philip, I record them as wholly true; where their accounts differ, I have chosen the version that seemed to me the more trustworthy and at the same time the more worth telling.

It is said that Philip died in the archonship of Pythodelus at Athens, and that Alexander, the son of Philip, then about twenty years of age, succeeded to the kingdom and at once went into the Peloponnese.

Alexander sent the booty back to the cities on the coast, handing it over to Lysanias and Philotas to dispose of. He himself crossed the summit and advanced through the Haemus into the country of the Triballians, and came to the river Lyginus, which is three days' march distant from the Ister for one travelling towards the Haemus.

On the third day after the battle Alexander reached the river Ister, the greatest of the rivers of Europe, traversing the most land and shutting off the most warlike peoples—mostly Celtic, where indeed its sources rise, the last of whom are the Quadi and Marcomanni;

They crossed by night where there was a deep field of standing grain, and so the more easily reached the bank unobserved. At dawn Alexander led on through the grain, ordering the infantry to bend down the corn with their sarissas held aslant, and so advance to the uncultivated ground. The cavalry followed as long as the phalanx went on through the grain;

He himself advanced into the country of the Agrianians and Paeonians. There messengers reached him reporting that Cleitus, son of Bardylis, had revolted, and that Glaucias, king of the Taulantians, had joined him; some reported also that the Autariatae would attack him on the march. For these reasons he resolved to break camp in haste.
The depth of the phalanx was one hundred and twenty; on either wing he posted two hundred cavalry, and ordered them to keep silence and to take the word of command sharply when it was given.

Meanwhile some of the exiles who had fled from Thebes, entering the city by night at the invitation of certain men within who wished to revolt, seized and killed Amyntas and Timolaus, two of those holding the Cadmeia, who suspected nothing hostile, outside the citadel.

But Ptolemy son of Lagus says that Perdiccas, posted in advance to guard the camp with his own battalion, not far from the enemy's stockade, without waiting for Alexander's signal for battle, was himself the first to attack the stockade, and tearing it apart broke in upon the Theban outpost.

This calamity of a Greek city, by the greatness of the captured city and the swiftness of the event, struck both the sufferers and the doers, and no less the other Greeks than those who shared in the deed itself, with consternation.

When the Thebans' fate was reported to the other Greeks, the Arcadians, as many as had set out from home to help the Thebans, condemned to death those who had induced them to the aid; the Eleans recalled their exiles, because they were well-disposed to Alexander;

Having accomplished these things, Alexander returned to Macedonia. He offered to Olympian Zeus the sacrifice established since the time of Archelaus, and held the Olympic games at Aegae; some say he held games in honour of the Muses as well.

As he went up to Ilium, Menoetius the pilot crowned him with a golden crown, and after him Chares the Athenian, coming from Sigeium, and certain others, some Greeks, some of the country. Others say that he also crowned the tomb of Achilles, and that Hephaestion, they say, crowned the tomb of Patroclus. And Alexander, as the story goes, counted Achilles happy in having Homer as the herald of his fame to later memory.

Meanwhile Alexander advanced upon the river Granicus with his army in order: he drew up the phalanx of the hoplites in a double line, led the cavalry on the wings, and ordered the baggage to follow behind. Hegelochus led those who were to reconnoitre the enemy in advance, having the lancer cavalry and about five hundred light troops.

Having said this, he sent Parmenion to command the left wing, while he himself went to the right. There were posted in advance, on the right, Philotas son of Parmenion, with the Companion cavalry, the archers, and the Agrianian javelin-men; Amyntas son of Arrhabaeus, with the lancer cavalry, was posted with Philotas, and the Paeonians and the squadron of Socrates.

The Persians, where Amyntas and Socrates first reached the bank, themselves hurled missiles from above—some casting javelins from the bank, from the higher ground, into the river, others going down along its lower parts to the very water.

And the Persians, now struck on every side in the face, both themselves and their horses, by the spears, and thrust back by the cavalry, and harmed too by the light troops mingled among the cavalry, gave way first at the point where Alexander fought in the forefront. When the centre had given way, the wings of the cavalry on either side were broken too, and then there was a headlong flight. Of the Persian cavalry about a thousand were killed.

Having appointed Calas to be satrap of the province Arsites had governed, and having ordered the same tributes to be paid as had been paid to Darius, he bade those barbarians who came down from the mountains and surrendered themselves to depart, each to his own home.

Meanwhile men came to him from Magnesia and Tralles surrendering their cities; and he sent Parmenion, giving him two thousand five hundred foot of the mercenaries, about as many Macedonians, and about two hundred of the Companion cavalry. He sent Alcimachus son of Agathocles to the Aeolian cities with a force no smaller, and to all the Ionian cities that were still under the barbarians.

Meanwhile Glaucippus, a man of repute in Miletus, sent to Alexander by the people and the mercenaries—to whom rather the city had been entrusted—said that the Milesians were willing to offer their walls and harbours in common to Alexander and the Persians, and asked that on these terms he raise the siege.

Alexander resolved to disband his fleet, both for lack of money at the time and because he saw his own fleet was no match for the Persian, and so he was unwilling to risk any part of his force. Besides, he reckoned that, now holding Asia with his land army, he no longer needed a fleet, and that by taking the coastal cities he would dissolve the Persian fleet, since they would have nowhere to recruit their crews nor any point of Asia to make for. Thus too he interpreted the eagle, that it had signified he would master the ships from the land.

Not many days later two Macedonian hoplites of Perdiccas' battalion, messing together and drinking together, each extolled himself and his own deeds greatly in talk. Then a rivalry seized them, and the wine too warmed them somewhat, so that, arming themselves, on their own account they assaulted the wall at the citadel turned most towards Mylasa, more to display their own strength than to make the contest against the enemy with danger.

Not many days later, as Alexander again brought up his engines against the inner brick wall and was himself overseeing the work, there was a sally in full force from the city: some by the ruined wall, where Alexander himself was posted, others by the Triple Gate, where the Macedonians were not at all expecting it.

Then the Persian commanders, Orontobates and Memnon, meeting together and judging from the circumstances that they could not hold out long under the siege—seeing part of the wall already fallen, part shaken down, and many of the soldiers either killed in the sallies or disabled by wounds—

There were some of the Macedonians serving with Alexander who had married shortly before the expedition; and Alexander judged that these too were not to be neglected, but sent them away from Caria to winter in Macedonia with their wives, appointing over them Ptolemy son of Seleucus, one of the royal bodyguards, and of the generals Coenus son of Polemocrates and Meleager son of Neoptolemus, because they too were among the newly wed;

While he was still about Phaselis, it was reported that Alexander son of Aëropus was plotting against him—a man who was among the Companions and at that time commanded the Thessalian cavalry. This Alexander was brother of Heromenes and Arrhabaeus, who had shared in the murder of Philip;

Alexander, setting out from Phaselis, sent part of his army through the mountains to Perge, where the Thracians had made a road for him through a passage otherwise difficult and long; he himself led those about him along the sea, by the shore. This road is passable only when the winds blow from the north; if south winds prevail, it is impossible to travel along the shore.

The greater part of Aspendus is built upon a strong and sheer height, and beside the very height the river Eurymedon flows; but they had also, around the height in the low ground, no few dwellings, with a wall, not great, thrown round them.

There came to him envoys of the Selgians. These too are Pisidian barbarians and dwell in a great city, and are themselves warlike; but because they happened to be enemies of the Telmissians from of old, they had sent an embassy to Alexander concerning friendship. With these Alexander made a treaty, and thereafter found them faithful in all things.

Thence he went towards Phrygia, past the lake named Ascania, in which salt forms of itself, and the inhabitants use it and have no need of the sea for this purpose; and on the fifth day he reached Celaenae. At Celaenae there was a citadel, sheer on every side, held by a garrison from the satrap of Phrygia—a thousand Carians and a hundred Greek mercenaries.

After this Memnon, who had been appointed by King Darius commander of the whole fleet and of all the coast, intending to turn the war back upon Macedonia and Greece, took Chios, surrendered to him by treachery. Sailing thence to Lesbos, when the Mytilenaeans would not yield to him, he won over the other cities of Lesbos.

Having done this, Pharnabazus sailed for Lycia, taking the mercenaries with him, while Autophradates sailed to the other islands. Meanwhile Darius sent down Thymondas son of Mentor, to take over the mercenaries from Pharnabazus and bring them up to the King, and to tell Pharnabazus that he should command all that Memnon had commanded.
When Alexander came to Gordium, a longing seized him to go up to the citadel, where the palace of Gordius and of his son Midas was, and to see the wagon of Gordius and the knot of the wagon's yoke.

The next day he set out for Ancyra in Galatia; and there an embassy of the Paphlagonians came to him, submitting their nation and making terms; but they begged him not to invade their country with his army.

—which mark the boundary between the country of the Cilicians and the Assyrians, to seize them beforehand and guard the passage, giving him the allied foot, the Greek mercenaries, the Thracians, led by Sitalces, and the Thessalian cavalry.

While he was still at Mallus, it was reported to him that Darius was encamped at Sochi with his whole force. This place is in the land of Assyria, distant about two days' march from the Assyrian Gates. Then, gathering the Companions, he told them what had been reported about Darius and Darius' army; and they bade him lead them on at once just as they were.

Crossing the mountain by the so-called Amanic Gates, Darius advanced towards Issus, and came, unobserved, in Alexander's rear. Seizing Issus, those of the Macedonians who had been left there sick he cruelly maltreated and killed; and on the next day he advanced to the river Pinarus.

He then gave orders for the men to take their meal, and sent on towards the Gates a few of the cavalry and of the archers to reconnoitre the road back; and he himself, in the night, taking his whole army, marched to hold the Gates again.

Meanwhile Alexander, seeing that nearly all the Persian cavalry had shifted to his left, towards the sea, while on that side only the Peloponnesians and the other allied cavalry were posted, sent the Thessalian cavalry quickly to the left, ordering them not to ride past the front of the whole array, lest they be seen by the enemy shifting, but to pass unseen behind the phalanx.

Drawn up thus, he led on for a time, pausing, so that his advance seemed quite leisurely; for Darius no longer led the barbarians forward, as they had first been posted, but stayed on the banks of the river, in many places sheer, and in some places he extended a palisade along them where they seemed easier of approach; and by this he at once made plain to Alexander's men that he was enslaved in spirit.

Meanwhile the battalions of the right wing, seeing the Persians opposite them already routed, wheeled against Darius' mercenaries and their own hard-pressed part, thrust them from the river, and, having outflanked the broken part of the Persian army, charged in upon their flank and were now cutting down the mercenaries.

The next day, though wounded in the thigh by a sword, Alexander visited the wounded, and gathering the dead, buried them magnificently with his whole force drawn up as splendidly as for war; and he honoured with a speech all whom he had himself seen do some signal deed in the battle, or had learned of by report agreed upon, and rewarded each with gifts of money according to his desert.

Darius fled that night with a few about him; and by day, picking up continually those of the Persians who had escaped from the battle and of the mercenaries, having about four thousand in all, he hastened towards the city of Thapsacus and the river Euphrates, to put the Euphrates as quickly as possible between himself and Alexander.
While Alexander was still at Marathus, there came from Darius envoys bringing a letter from Darius, and themselves to beg by word of mouth for the release to Darius of his mother, wife, and children.

Thus he wrote to Darius. When he learned that the treasure which Darius had sent off with Cophen son of Artabazus to Damascus had been captured, and that all the Persians left in charge of it, with the rest of the royal state, had likewise been taken, he ordered Parmenion to bring them back to Damascus and guard them.

For there is in Tyre a temple of Heracles, the most ancient of those whose memory is preserved among men, not of the Argive Heracles son of Alcmene; for Heracles is honoured in Tyre many generations before Cadmus, setting out from Phoenicia, took Thebes, and the daughter Semele was born to Cadmus, from whom Dionysus son of Zeus was born.

march to Egypt is not safe while the Persians command the sea, nor to pursue Darius leaving behind us the city of the Tyrians in doubtful allegiance and Egypt and Cyprus held by the Persians—this too is not safe, especially with regard to the affairs of Greece;

Speaking thus, he easily persuaded them to attempt Tyre. And something divine too persuaded him, that on that very night he dreamed that he was advancing to the wall of the Tyrians, and that Heracles took him by the right hand and led him up into the city. And Aristander interpreted this as meaning that Tyre would be taken with toil, since the deeds of Heracles too were done with toil. And indeed the siege of Tyre appeared a great work.

Filling a horse-transport ship with dry brushwood and other easily burnt material, they fixed two masts on the prow and fenced it round on either side as widely as possible, so as to hold thereon as much chaff and as many torches as could be received; and on it they heaped pitch, sulphur, and whatever else might kindle a great flame.

and Enylus of Byblus, when they learned that their cities were held by Alexander, left Autophradates and the ships with him and came to Alexander with their own fleet, and the Sidonian triremes with them, so that about eighty Phoenician ships came to him.

By now, many engineers having been gathered from Cyprus and all Phoenicia, many engines had been put together, some on the mole, some on the horse-transport ships, which he had brought with him from Sidon, and some on the triremes of his that were not fast sailers.
It happened that on that day Alexander had withdrawn to his tent, but had not lingered as was his wont, but returned after a short time to the ships.

On the third day after this, watching for a calm and exhorting the leaders of the battalions to the work, he brought the engines on the ships against the city. First he shook the wall greatly, and when the breach appeared sufficient in breadth, he ordered the engine-bearing ships to draw off;

Those on the ships—the Phoenicians by the harbour towards Egypt, where they happened to be blockading, forcing their way and tearing apart the barriers, shattered the ships in the harbour, charging some in deep water, driving others ashore; and the Cyprians, by the other harbour leading from Sidon, which had no barrier, sailing in, took the city at once on that side.

While Alexander was still engaged in the siege of Tyre, there came to him envoys from Darius, announcing that Darius was willing to give Alexander ten thousand talents for his mother, wife, and children; that all the country within the river Euphrates as far as the Greek sea should be Alexander's; and that, marrying the daughter of Darius, Alexander should be a friend and ally of Darius.

Gaza is distant from the sea about twenty stades, and the approach to it is sandy and deep, and the sea by the city is all shoaly. Gaza was a great city, built on a high mound, and a strong wall was thrown round it. It was the last settled place as one goes from Phoenicia towards Egypt, at the edge of the desert.

out of range. But when there was a strong sally from the city, and the Arabs brought fire against the engines, and from the higher ground shot at and thrust down the mole the Macedonians who defended themselves from below, then Alexander, either willingly disobeying the seer or in the heat of the work forgetting the prophecy, took the hypaspists and went to the rescue where the Macedonians were most hard pressed.

Alexander now set out for Egypt, where he had first purposed to go, and on the seventh day, marching from Gaza, he came to Pelusium in Egypt. His fleet sailed along the coast from Phoenicia towards Egypt, and he found the ships lying at anchor at Pelusium.

There is also told a story of this kind, not incredible to me: that Alexander wished to leave the marks of the fortification for the builders, but there was nothing with which to mark out the ground; whereupon one of the builders bethought himself, and gathering the barley-meal which the soldiers carried in their vessels, threw it down on the ground where the king directed; and so the circle of the wall he was making for the city was traced out.

After this a longing seized him to go to Ammon in Libya, partly to consult the god, since the oracle of Ammon was said to be unerring, and Perseus and Heracles had consulted it—the one when he was sent by Polydectes against the Gorgon, the other when he went against Antaeus in Libya and against Busiris in Egypt.

The place where the temple of Ammon is has all around it desert and sand and no water; but it itself, small in the midst—for at its widest it extends to about forty stades—is full of cultivated trees, olives and date-palms, and alone of all the region is bedewed.

At Memphis many embassies came to him from Greece, and there was none whom he sent away unsuccessful in what he asked; and an army came to him—from Antipater, Greek mercenaries about four hundred, led by Menoetas son of Hegesander, and from Thrace cavalry about five hundred, commanded by Asclepiodorus son of Eunicus.

At the first showing of spring Alexander marched from Memphis towards Phoenicia; and the passage of the Nile at Memphis and all its canals were bridged for him. When he came to Tyre, he found that his fleet had already come to him there. At Tyre he again sacrificed to Heracles and held a contest in athletics and music.

in the archonship of Aristophanes at Athens; and he found the passage bridged with two bridges. For Mazaeus, to whom the guard of the river had been entrusted by Darius, having about three thousand cavalry and of these two thousand Greek mercenary foot, had till then kept guard there on the river;

Taking the royal squadron, one of the Companions, and the Paeonian scouts, he drove on in haste, and ordered the rest of the army to follow at a walk. The Persian cavalry, seeing Alexander's men coming on sharply, fled at full speed. Alexander pursued and pressed them;

When this was reported to Alexander by the Persian scouts who were captured, he remained where it was reported for four days; and he rested the army from the march, and fortified the camp with a ditch and a palisade. For he resolved to leave the baggage and those of the soldiers unfit for fighting, and himself to go into the contest with the fighting men carrying nothing but their arms.

Having exhorted them with these and a few other such words, and been exhorted in turn by the leaders to take heart in them, he ordered the army to take their meal and rest. Parmenion, they say, came to him at his tent and advised him to attack the Persians by night; for he would fall upon them unexpected and disordered, and at the same time more terrible by night.

Darius and the army with Darius remained drawn up through the night just as they had first been arranged, because they had no proper camp thrown round them, and at the same time feared lest the enemy attack them by night.

He posted also a second line, so that the phalanx should be two-fronted. And it was enjoined upon the leaders of the rear ranks that, if they should see their own men encircled by the Persian army, they should wheel about and receive the barbarians;

When the armies were now near, Darius and those about him were seen—the apple-bearer Persians, the Indians, the Albanians, the deported Carians, and the Mardian archers, posted opposite Alexander himself and the royal squadron. Alexander led rather towards his own right, and the Persians moved opposite him, far outflanking him on their left.
As Darius now led on his whole phalanx, Alexander ordered Aretes to charge those who were riding round their right wing to encircle it;

At this point, the Macedonians being at first assailed on both sides, Parmenion sent in haste to Alexander to report that his part was hard pressed and that help was needed. When this was reported to Alexander, he turned aside from the pursuit, and wheeling with the Companion cavalry led at a run against the right of the barbarians. First he charged the fleeing enemy cavalry, the Parthyaeans, some of the Indians, and the most numerous and strongest of the Persians.

Darius, straight from the battle, drove along the mountains of the Armenians towards Media; and with him fled the Bactrian cavalry, as they had been drawn up in the battle, and of the Persians the kinsmen of the king and a few of the so-called apple-bearers.

Setting out from Susa and crossing the river Pasitigris, he invaded the land of the Uxians. Of the Uxians, those dwelling in the plains obeyed the satrap of the Persians, and now surrendered to Alexander; but the so-called mountain Uxians were not subjects of the Persians, and now, sending to Alexander, said that they would not let him pass on his way to Persia with his force unless he paid them what they had been wont to receive from the king of the Persians for the passage.

After this he sent the baggage, the Thessalian cavalry, the allies, the mercenaries, and all the rest of the army more heavily armed, with Parmenion, to go towards Persia by the wagon-road leading to Persia.

Having done this, he advanced towards Media; for there he learned that Darius was. Darius had resolved that, if Alexander stayed at Susa and Babylon, he too would await him there in Media, in case any revolution should arise among Alexander's people; but if Alexander marched against him, he would go up-country towards the Parthyaeans and Hyrcania, as far as Bactra, laying waste all the country and making the road forward impassable for Alexander.

He himself, taking the Companion cavalry, the scouts, the mercenary cavalry, led by Erigyius, the Macedonian phalanx except those posted over the money, the archers, and the Agrianians, drove on against Darius. On the way, made in haste, many of the soldiers fell behind through exhaustion, and horses died;

Meanwhile there came to him from Darius' camp Bagistanes, a Babylonian, a man of note, and with him Antibelus, one of the sons of Mazaeus. These reported that Nabarzanes, chiliarch of the cavalry fleeing with Darius, and Bessus the satrap of the Bactrians, and Barsaentes the satrap of the Arachotians and Drangians, had arrested Darius.

Alexander sent the body of Darius to Persia, bidding it be buried in the royal tombs, like the other kings before Darius; and he appointed as satrap of the Parthyaeans and Hyrcanians Amminapes, a Parthyaean; this man was one of those who had surrendered Egypt to Alexander with Mazaces. Tlepolemus son of Pythophanes, one of the Companions, was joined with him to oversee affairs among the Parthyaeans and Hyrcanians.

Alexander, taking up those of the army left behind in the pursuit, advanced into Hyrcania. The country of Hyrcania lies on the left of the road leading to Bactra; on one side it is shut off by thick and high mountains, but its plain reaches down to the great sea there. He led this way because he learned that the mercenaries with Darius had escaped this way to the mountains of the Tapurians, and at the same time to subdue the Tapurians themselves.

He himself advanced against the Mardians, taking the hypaspists, the archers, the Agrianians, the battalion of Coenus and Amyntas, half of the Companion cavalry, and the mounted javelin-men; for he now had a unit of mounted javelin-men.

Having done this, he marched towards Zadracarta, the greatest city of Hyrcania, where the palace of the Hyrcanians was. There, spending fifteen days and sacrificing to the gods according to custom and holding an athletic contest, he marched towards the Parthyaeans; and thence to the borders of Areia and to Susia, a city of Areia, where Satibarzanes too, the satrap of the Areians, came to him.

There too Alexander learned of the plot of Philotas son of Parmenion; and Ptolemy and Aristobulus say that it had been reported to him before, in Egypt, but had not appeared trustworthy, both for the sake of the old friendship and the honour shown by him to Parmenion the father of Philotas and his trust in Philotas himself.

They say too that Amyntas son of Andromenes was brought to trial at the same time, and Polemon, Attalus, and Simmias, the brothers of Amyntas, as having themselves shared in the plot against Alexander, through their loyalty and comradeship with Philotas.

Having done this, he advanced towards Bactra and Bessus, subduing on the way the Drangians and Gadrosians. He subdued also the Arachotians and appointed Menon satrap over them. He overran too the Indians neighbouring the Arachotians. All these nations he overran through deep snow and amid scarcity of supplies and hardship of the soldiers.

the army, led to Aornus and Bactra, which are the greatest cities in the Bactrian country. These he took at the first assault, and left a garrison in the citadel of Aornus, and over it Archelaus son of Androcles of the Companions; and over the other Bactrians, who submitted without difficulty, he appointed as satrap Artabazus the Persian. He himself marched towards the river Oxus.

There Ptolemy learned that Spitamenes and Dataphernes were not firm in their resolve about the surrender of Bessus. So he left the foot, ordering them to follow in order, and himself, riding with the cavalry, came to a certain village where Bessus was with a few soldiers.

Not many days later there came to Alexander envoys from the Scythians called the Abii (whom Homer too in his poem praised as the most just of men; they dwell in Asia, independent, in no small part because of their poverty and their justice), and also from the European Scythians, who are the greatest of the Scythian nations settled in Europe.

In this country, which Alexander traversed between the rivers Cophen and Indus, the city of Nysa also is said to have been founded; and the founding of it was the work of Dionysus, who built Nysa at the time when he had subdued the Indians—whenever that was, and from whatever point he set out against them.

When there had been prepared for Alexander on the banks of the Hydaspes many thirty-oared galleys and vessels of one-and-a-half banks, and many horse-transports too, and other craft suited for the conveyance of an army by river, he resolved to sail down the Hydaspes toward the great sea. For previously, seeing crocodiles in the river Indus,

When Alexander had come to Pasargadae and to Persepolis, a longing seized him to sail down the Euphrates and the Tigris to the Persian Sea, and to behold the mouths of these rivers as he had beheld that of the Indus and the sea there.

With these envoys Alexander sent some of the Companions, ostensibly as an embassy to establish friendship, though the real purpose of the mission was rather to reconnoitre the nature of the Scythian country, the size of their population, their customs, and the equipment with which they take the field for battle.

For I cannot determine who this Dionysus was, nor whether it was the Theban Dionysus who, setting out from Thebes, or from Tmolus in Lydia, came against the Indians at the head of an army, passing through so many warlike nations unknown to the Greeks of that day, yet subduing none of them by force save only the Indians. But this much may be said: a man ought not to be too exacting an examiner of the ancient tales told concerning the divine. For things which, judged by mere probability, seem incredible, do not appear wholly incredible once one has added the working of the divine to the account.

the only river except the Nile in which they occur, and seeing along the banks of the Acesines beans growing of the kind that the Egyptian land produces, and having heard that the Acesines empties into the Indus, he thought he had discovered the sources of the Nile;

Some have recorded this also: that Alexander purposed to sail round the greater part of Arabia, and the land of the Ethiopians, and Libya, and the Numidians beyond Mount Atlas, as far as Gadeira and inward into our own sea; and that, having subdued Libya and Carthage, he would then with justice be called king of all Asia.

He himself resolved to found a city beside the river Tanais, and to give it his own name. For the site seemed to him suitable for the city to grow large, and well placed for an expedition against the Scythians, should one ever prove necessary, and for the protection of the country against the raids of the barbarians who dwelt beyond the river.

When Alexander came up to Nysa, the people of Nysa sent out to him the foremost man among them, whose name was Acuphis, and with him thirty of their most reputable envoys, to beg Alexander to leave the city free for the sake of the god.

namely, that the Nile rose here somewhere out of the Indians, and flowing through much desert land there lost the name of Indus, and then, where it begins to flow through inhabited country, was called the Nile by the Ethiopians of those parts and by the Egyptians, or, as Homer made it, Aegyptus after Egypt, and so discharged into the inner sea.

For the kings of the Persians and the Medes, he said, who ruled not even the smallest portion of Asia, had no just claim to call themselves Great Kings. From this point some say that he intended to sail into the Euxine Sea, against the Scythians and to Lake Maeotis; others, that he meant to go to Sicily and the Iapygian promontory, for already the name of the Romans, advancing to greatness, was beginning to stir him.

He thought too that the city would become great both from the number of those settled in it and from the splendour of its name. Meanwhile the barbarians who lived along the river seized and killed the Macedonian soldiers who were holding the garrisons in their cities, and began to fortify the cities the more strongly for their own security.

The envoys, it is said, entered Alexander's tent and found him seated, still covered with dust from the march and still in his armour, with his helmet on his head and his spear in his hand; and they were astonished at the sight, and falling to the ground they kept silence for a long while. But when Alexander raised them up and bade them take heart, then at last Acuphis began to speak thus:

And indeed, writing to Olympias about the land of the Indians, among other things he wrote that he thought he had discovered the sources of the Nile, drawing his conclusions about such great matters from small and trivial signs.

For my own part, what Alexander's designs were I cannot affirm with certainty, nor does it concern me to make conjectures; but this much I think I myself can confidently maintain: that he planned nothing small or mean, and that he would never have remained at rest, content with any of the possessions he had already won, not even if he had added Europe to Asia and the islands of the Britons to Europe; but that he would still have sought beyond them for some unknown thing, vying, if with no other, then at least with himself.

This, sent by a great king to a man ruling over much land and many men, and moreover to a bad man, I cannot praise.
